questions.q: Why can't an atom really be a tiny solar system, with electrons orbiting the nucleus like planets?
options: An orbiting charge gives off light, so the electron would lose energy and spiral into the nucleus almost at once
The nucleus attracts the electron so strongly that it would be pulled to one fixed orbit and stop moving
The electron's charge would cancel the nucleus's charge, so the atom would fall apart into separate particles
An orbiting electron would gain energy from each turn and soon fly out of the atom altogether
questions.explain: Classical physics says a charge moving in a circle radiates light. An orbiting electron would lose energy and spiral in within about 10⁻¹¹ s, yet atoms are stable with only certain energies. At this scale classical physics is simply wrong.

questions.q: The picture shows the photoelectric effect. Bright red light knocks out no electrons, but dim blue light does. What does this show?
questions.alt: Left: many waves of bright red light hit a metal and no electrons come out. Right: two waves of dim blue light hit the metal and electrons fly out
options: Light comes in packets (photons), and one blue photon carries more energy than one red photon
Red light is absorbed by the air before it reaches the metal, so it never arrives
Bright light pushes the electrons back into the metal, while dim light lets them escape
Metals only respond to blue light because they are blue-coloured inside
questions.explain: Einstein (1905): light arrives in packets, photons. Each blue photon has enough energy to free an electron; a red photon does not, and adding more red photons does not help.

questions.q: Light spreads out after passing through a narrow gap, like ripples on a pond. What is this called, and what does it show?
options: Diffraction: it shows that light travels as a wave
Reflection: it shows that light bounces off the edges of the gap
Absorption: it shows that the gap takes energy from the light
The photoelectric effect: it shows that light is made of particles
questions.explain: Spreading out after a narrow gap is diffraction, a sure sign of a wave. Light travels like a wave and arrives like a particle: wave–particle duality.

questions.q: De Broglie said everything that moves has a wavelength, equal to h divided by its momentum. Why do we never see a baseball diffract?
options: Its momentum is so large that its wavelength is far smaller than an atomic nucleus
Baseballs are made of atoms, and atoms cannot have a wavelength
Its wavelength is so large that it covers the whole stadium
Only charged particles such as electrons have a wavelength
questions.explain: Wavelength = h / momentum. Heavy, fast things have tiny wavelengths: a baseball's is far smaller than a nucleus. An electron's is a few nanometres, about the size of a transistor, so electrons in devices behave as waves.

questions.q: In the two-slit experiment, electrons are sent one at a time. What builds up on the screen?
options: Each electron lands as a single dot, but over many electrons the dots form the stripes of a wave pattern
Each electron spreads out over the whole screen as a faint cloud
The electrons form two bright stripes, one behind each slit, like tiny balls
Nothing appears, because a single electron cannot pass through two slits
questions.explain: Each electron is detected as a dot (a particle), but the dots build up interference stripes (a wave). The wave sets the chances; the particle is what we detect.

questions.q: What does the wave ψ in the Schrödinger equation tell us about an electron?
options: ψ² gives the chance of finding the electron at each place
ψ² gives the exact path the electron follows
ψ² gives the electron's speed at each place
ψ² gives the electric charge of the electron at each place
questions.explain: We never see the wave itself. The chance of finding the electron at a place follows ψ², the wave squared (Born's rule).

questions.q: Why can a trapped electron only have certain energies?
options: Its wave must fit inside the box, like a guitar string pinned at both ends, so only whole numbers of humps are allowed
The walls absorb any electron that has the wrong energy, so only electrons with certain energies are left inside the box
The electron loses a little energy at each bounce off the walls, until it settles at one of a few fixed values
The box's atoms each hold one electron, so only as many energies as there are atoms are allowed
questions.explain: Like a string fixed at both ends, the electron's wave must fit the box: only whole numbers of humps. Each fit has its own energy, so the energy is quantised. More humps mean tighter wiggles and more energy.

questions.q: An electron is trapped in a box. If the width of the box is halved, what happens to each allowed energy?
options: It becomes four times larger
It becomes twice as large
It becomes half as large
It does not change
questions.explain: The allowed energies go as 1/(width)², so halving the box makes every energy four times larger. In a nanostructure, size sets energy.

questions.q: The top of the picture shows ψ² for the two lowest states in a box; the dots below are 900 looks at where the electron is. Where is the electron in the second state never found?
questions.alt: Two boxes: for n = 1 the curve ψ² has one hump and the dots of 900 looks cluster in one group; for n = 2 the curve has two humps and the dots form two groups
options: Exactly in the middle of the box
Close to the left wall of the box
In the two humps either side of the middle
It is found equally often everywhere in the box
questions.explain: For n = 2, ψ² is zero at the centre, so the electron is never found exactly in the middle. Each look finds the whole electron at one place; the curve is the pattern over many looks.

questions.q: True or false: a trapped electron can never be completely still, even in its lowest-energy state.
options: True
False
questions.explain: True. There is no state with zero humps (no n = 0), so the lowest energy is above zero. A wave squeezed into a box must wiggle: a trapped electron can never sit still.

questions.q: The picture shows the levels in a large, a medium and a small quantum dot of the same material. Why does the small dot give out bluer light?
questions.alt: Three boxes of decreasing width, labelled large, medium and small dot, each with two levels and a wavy arrow of light: red (640 nm), green (560 nm) and blue (470 nm)
options: Squeezing the box pushes the levels further apart, so an electron dropping between them gives out a higher-energy photon
A small dot is made of a material with a larger band gap, so the light it gives out has more energy
A small dot holds fewer electrons, so each photon it gives out is shared among fewer of them and has more energy
A small dot has more surface atoms, and surface atoms always give out blue light
questions.explain: A smaller box pushes the levels up and apart. The bigger the gap the electron drops across, the higher the photon's energy and the bluer the light: same material, different size, different colour.

questions.q: At room temperature, every electron is jostled by about 26 meV of thermal energy. When do the quantised levels in a box actually show up?
options: When the levels are much further apart than 26 meV, so the thermal jostling cannot blur them together
When the levels are much closer together than 26 meV, so the thermal jostling can mix them
Always, whatever the size of the box and the temperature
Never at room temperature: only near absolute zero
questions.explain: Levels closer than the thermal jostling of about 26 meV blur together; levels well apart stand out. In GaAs this means boxes narrower than about 15–20 nm, so the structures of Lecture 2 are a few to a few tens of nanometres.
